voice.refText: Twice a week, you sell your plasma, the pale part of your blood. It's the most the law allows. That's the band. A thin strip you wear across your forehead. While you sleep, it lends your brain to a company. And it pays you, by the hour.

Waitress.describe: A quick, bright female mezzo: a diner waitress in her thirties. Dry, wry and fast, a pencil-behind-the-ear voice that has heard every excuse, flat American vowels, a smile under the sarcasm.

Marco.describe: A young, warm male tenor: a short-order cook in his late twenties. Slightly hoarse, easygoing and quick to laugh, cheeky, a little breathless, a working man's casual American English.

Plant boss.describe: A big, booming male baritone: a car-plant boss in his fifties. Confident and loud, a salesman's warmth, quick to laugh at his own jokes, a voice used to talking over machinery.

Banker.describe: A smooth, precise male tenor: a small-town bank manager in his sixties. Polite, slightly pompous, every consonant crisp, a man pleased to correct you.

Mayor.describe: A clear, ringing female alto: a small-town mayor in her fifties. Warm and public, a speech-giver's lift on every line, upbeat and a little too sure of herself.

Rival.describe: A low, gravelly female voice: a diner owner in her sixties across town. Husky, blunt and sardonic, slow and knowing, a smoker's rasp, never impressed.

Plumber.describe: A deep, slow male bass: a plumber in his forties. Unhurried, stubborn and amused, few words and every one final, a man who knows nobody else can fix the sink.

Reporter.describe: A bright, fast female soprano: a local TV reporter in her twenties. Eager and clipped, a broadcaster's projection, every question pitched up like a headline.

lines.text: What if you fired everyone and hired AI? Six weeks from now, you're the richest person this town has ever had. And its last customer.
lines.say: [sly, close, a dare with a grin behind it, then a beat, quick and thrilled, the last three words dropped low] What if you fired everyone and hired AI? Six weeks from now, you're the richest person this town has ever had. And its last customer.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Waitress: Marco's sick. Again.
lines.say: [flat, fed up, holding the phone out like a bad fish] Marco's sick. Again.
lines.speaker: Waitress

lines.text: Marco: It isn't me. It's Mondays.
lines.say: [croaky, aggrieved, a fake cough swallowed before the second sentence] It isn't me. It's Mondays.
lines.speaker: Marco

lines.text: Waitress: It's the fourth Monday, Marco. What do I tell forty stools?
lines.say: [flat, fed up, the phone held out like a bad fish, the question thrown at him] It's the fourth Monday, Marco. What do I tell forty stools?
lines.speaker: Waitress

lines.text: Marco: Tell them Tuesday.
lines.say: [quick, breezy, no beat at all, already hanging up, crisp and clear, every word distinct, no laughter] Tell them Tuesday.
lines.speaker: Marco

lines.text: Waitress: Marco? A cook just walked in. A steel one. He's doing your job, and he's better at it.
lines.say: [stunned, small, the phone snatched back off the floor, each sentence a fresh shock, a cruel little relish on the last clause] Marco? A cook just walked in. A steel one. He's doing your job, and he's better at it.
lines.speaker: Waitress

lines.text: Marco: Is he on the payroll?
lines.say: [the croak gone, sharp, the only question that matters to him] Is he on the payroll?
lines.speaker: Marco

lines.text: He isn't. That's the whole offer. So what if you could hire a machine for any job in town, for nothing at all?
lines.say: [dry, delighted, a secret told quick, then conspiratorial and close, the last four words savoured] He isn't. That's the whole offer. So what if you could hire a machine for any job in town, for nothing at all?
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Every lunch, the same count. The whistle, forty overalls across the road, forty stools full, one finger each. You have never once wondered where the overalls get the money.
lines.say: [brisk, fond, counting on fingers, satisfied on each forty, then slower and teasing, a finger wagged at you on the last sentence] Every lunch, the same count. The whistle, forty overalls across the road, forty stools full, one finger each. You have never once wondered where the overalls get the money.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: The rule is three lines. Type a job, and by the next shift a machine worker is at your door. No wage, no sleep, no mistakes. Hire as many as you like, and rent them to anyone who asks. And the app has one dial, for every machine at once: what a shift costs whoever rents it. Only you can turn it, and the moment you do, any renter can walk away. Remember that.
lines.say: [clear, clipped, a card laid on the table, each of the three nos a hammer tap, generous on the renting, then measured and slower on the dial, the last two words almost a whisper] The rule is three lines. Type a job, and by the next shift a machine worker is at your door. No wage, no sleep, no mistakes. Hire as many as you like, and rent them to anyone who asks. And the app has one dial, for every machine at once: what a shift costs whoever rents it. Only you can turn it, and the moment you do, any renter can walk away. Remember that.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Waitress: So what does it eat?
lines.say: [curious, suspicious, leaning in close to the beaming screen] So what does it eat?
lines.speaker: Waitress

lines.text: Nothing. It never eats, and it never buys a slice of your pie. Right now that's the best part of the deal. By the sixth Friday it's the only part that matters.
lines.say: [flat on the first word, answering for the cook after its silence, then wry, then low and slow on the last sentence, a pin pushed into the map] Nothing. It never eats, and it never buys a slice of your pie. Right now that's the best part of the deal. By the sixth Friday it's the only part that matters.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: And Marco's cough clears up the second he hears the word robot. He's on his way in, with his own spatula.
lines.say: [amused, quick, a laugh under the first sentence, a dig on the spatula] And Marco's cough clears up the second he hears the word robot. He's on his way in, with his own spatula.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Marco: That's my grill.
lines.say: [out of breath, outraged, a burger sailing over his head] That's my grill.
lines.speaker: Marco

lines.text: Waitress: It was your grill on Mondays. Now it's his every day.
lines.say: [dry, a quick comeback, no pity in it, the second sentence slower] It was your grill on Mondays. Now it's his every day.
lines.speaker: Waitress

lines.text: Marco: We'll see.
lines.say: [grim, squaring up, spatula raised, a beat before he says it] We'll see.
lines.speaker: Marco

lines.text: Waitress: Marco. It's on your hat.
lines.say: [deadpan, a beat after the burger lands, the second sentence flat and slow] Marco. It's on your hat.
lines.speaker: Waitress

lines.text: Marco: It can't even taste it!
lines.say: [wounded, shouting, burger still on his hat] It can't even taste it!
lines.speaker: Marco

lines.text: You fire all three before the rush: Marco, your waitress, and the dishwasher, who left last year and never came back anyway. Three wages gone, burgers the same. You write it on a napkin. Money out is money out. Simple.
lines.say: [brisk, ruthless, a shrug of a joke on the dishwasher, then pleased with yourself, counting it off, the last word smug] You fire all three before the rush: Marco, your waitress, and the dishwasher, who left last year and never came back anyway. Three wages gone, burgers the same. You write it on a napkin. Money out is money out. Simple.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Then the whistle blows, and forty stools are fed before Marco has found his hat. On stool four, the man who runs the plant across the road, staring.
lines.say: [quick, gleeful, a dig on the hat, then slower, a camera finding him, the last word held] Then the whistle blows, and forty stools are fed before Marco has found his hat. On stool four, the man who runs the plant across the road, staring.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Plant boss: Where'd you get the cooks?
lines.say: [mouth half full, amazed, a man who smells money] Where'd you get the cooks?
lines.speaker: Plant boss

lines.text: Marco: Don't show him. Don't you dare show him.
lines.say: [urgent, hissed from the door, hat half over his face, the second sentence louder] Don't show him. Don't you dare show him.
lines.speaker: Marco

lines.text: You show him. And the plant across the road has four hundred people in it.
lines.say: [quick and gleeful on the first sentence, then slow, a hook sinking in, the number weighed] You show him. And the plant across the road has four hundred people in it.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: The boss rents fifty for his paint shop. The dial says cheap, so your phone pings once a shift, all night, under your pillow.
lines.say: [building, greedy, each ping a little faster, a grin on the pillow] The boss rents fifty for his paint shop. The dial says cheap, so your phone pings once a shift, all night, under your pillow.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Plant boss: They don't stop for lunch?
lines.say: [dazed, checking his watch, barely believing it] They don't stop for lunch?
lines.speaker: Plant boss

lines.text: They don't stop for anything. You'd think fifty machines means fifty fewer painters, and that's that. But a cheap shift is a cheap shift, so the boss runs three shifts where he ran one, rents five hundred, and writes your two lines on a napkin of his own.
lines.say: [deadpan on the first sentence, then leaning in, setting you up, a turn on but, escalating, a gasp of a laugh on the five hundred, ominous on the napkin] They don't stop for anything. You'd think fifty machines means fifty fewer painters, and that's that. But a cheap shift is a cheap shift, so the boss runs three shifts where he ran one, rents five hundred, and writes your two lines on a napkin of his own.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Marco: You hiring?
lines.say: [beaming, hopeful, hard hat sideways, brand-new overalls] You hiring?
lines.speaker: Marco

lines.text: Plant boss: Night shift. Somebody has to watch the machines.
lines.say: [clipped, a clipboard, not quite a kindness] Night shift. Somebody has to watch the machines.
lines.speaker: Plant boss

lines.text: Marco: What happened to watching?
lines.say: [small, crushed, the hard hat in his hands, crisp and clear, every word distinct, no laughter] What happened to watching?
lines.speaker: Marco

lines.text: Plant boss: I typed WATCHER.
lines.say: [flat, not meeting his eye, from the gatehouse window, a beat before it] I typed WATCHER.
lines.speaker: Plant boss

lines.text: And by now the whole town has heard where the plant got its painters.
lines.say: [brisk, the story moving on, a grin spreading on the last word] And by now the whole town has heard where the plant got its painters.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Banker: ATMs didn't kill tellers, you know.
lines.say: [smug, glasses up, a man quoting the one book he read] ATMs didn't kill tellers, you know.
lines.speaker: Banker

lines.text: Plant boss: Then what are you doing here?
lines.say: [mouth full, a quick comeback, a burger in each hand] Then what are you doing here?
lines.speaker: Plant boss

lines.text: Banker: Renting twelve.
lines.say: [smug, glasses up, straight back without a beat] Renting twelve.
lines.speaker: Banker

lines.text: Most people would guess the cash machines killed the tellers. They didn't. As cash machines spread across America, teller jobs rose, modestly, to about 550,000 by 2010. The machine counted the cash. It never asked about your mother's hip.
lines.say: [fair, conceding it with a raised eyebrow, the fact told as a surprise, a lift on rose, then warm and wry, the last sentence softer] Most people would guess the cash machines killed the tellers. They didn't. As cash machines spread across America, teller jobs rose, modestly, to about five hundred and fifty thousand by twenty ten. The machine counted the cash. It never asked about your mother's hip.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: His twelve ask about mothers' hips.
lines.say: [deadpan, a trap snapping shut, a laugh held under it] His twelve ask about mothers' hips.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Mayor: New jobs always come.
lines.say: [bright, practised, a sash and a wave] New jobs always come.
lines.speaker: Mayor

lines.text: Rival: Name one.
lines.say: [arms folded, sharp, straight back at her] Name one.
lines.speaker: Rival

lines.text: Mayor: Farming. Nobody farms any more, and nobody starved.
lines.say: [bright, practised, a sash and a wave, pleased with the answer] Farming. Nobody farms any more, and nobody starved.
lines.speaker: Mayor

lines.text: She's right too. In 1900 about 41 percent of American workers were on farms. A century later, under 2 percent. The new jobs came because people were still better at something. Here, whatever the new job is, somebody types it in.
lines.say: [steady, granting it, the numbers plain, a stress on better, then sly and quiet, a card turned over on the last sentence] She's right too. In nineteen hundred about forty-one percent of American workers were on farms. A century later, under two percent. The new jobs came because people were still better at something. Here, whatever the new job is, somebody types it in.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Rival: Eight cooks, please. And don't tell my customers.
lines.say: [brisk, the phone taken out of the mayor's hand, then hushed and guilty] Eight cooks, please. And don't tell my customers.
lines.speaker: Rival

lines.text: Your competition pays you rent. And by Friday every owner in town has done your sum on a napkin of their own and got the same answer. Nobody copied. Nobody had to.
lines.say: [gloating, quick, a laugh held under it, then cool, a fan of cards laid out, the last three words slow] Your competition pays you rent. And by Friday every owner in town has done your sum on a napkin of their own and got the same answer. Nobody copied. Nobody had to.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Plumber: I'm not typing my own job in.
lines.say: [gruff, amused, pushing the phone back with one finger] I'm not typing my own job in.
lines.speaker: Plumber

lines.text: He won't, the hairdresser won't, and everyone else is in the app by Friday.
lines.say: [brisk, ticking them off, a shrug on the last clause] He won't, the hairdresser won't, and everyone else is in the app by Friday.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Reporter: The town's first machine millionaire! How does it feel?
lines.say: [breathless, thrilled, microphone thrust forward, the question bright] The town's first machine millionaire! How does it feel?
lines.speaker: Reporter

lines.text: And six Fridays in, the plant pays its last human wage.
lines.say: [quiet, cold, the last three words spaced out] And six Fridays in, the plant pays its last human wage.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: The mayor hands you a key to the town the size of a loaf. And every truck that leaves for the next town makes you richer here, and leaves that town with fewer wages to spend.
lines.say: [grand, giddy, a laugh on the loaf, then a sly turn, the last clause quieter, a shadow on it] The mayor hands you a key to the town the size of a loaf. And every truck that leaves for the next town makes you richer here, and leaves that town with fewer wages to spend.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Reporter: Isn't this the dream? Nobody has to work!
lines.say: [bright, earnest, half to the camera, the second sentence a cheer] Isn't this the dream? Nobody has to work!
lines.speaker: Reporter

lines.text: Marco: Nobody has to. Nobody's allowed to.
lines.say: [from the crowd, flat, a beat after her, the second sentence slower and bitter, crisp and clear, every word distinct, no laughter] Nobody has to. Nobody's allowed to.
lines.speaker: Marco

lines.text: Someone did dream it. In 1930 the economist Keynes named technological unemployment, jobs lost because we save labour faster than we find new uses for it, a temporary phase, he called it. And in about a hundred years, about now, he guessed, a fifteen-hour week. He meant the work shared out and living standards kept. Here the hours went to the machines, and the pay went to you.
lines.say: [storyteller, measured, the name given with relish, a knowing lift on about now, then even, then pointed, the last word landed on you like a finger] Someone did dream it. In nineteen thirty the economist Keynes named technological unemployment, jobs lost because we save labour faster than we find new uses for it, a temporary phase, he called it. And in about a hundred years, about now, he guessed, a fifteen-hour week. He meant the work shared out and living standards kept. Here the hours went to the machines, and the pay went to you.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Then the sixth Friday. The whistle blows, the gate opens, and nobody comes out.
lines.say: [quiet, cold, each clause spaced, the last three words hollow] Then the sixth Friday. The whistle blows, the gate opens, and nobody comes out.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Forty stools, nobody on them. Every coin that ever crossed your counter came out of an overall's pocket, and you've just put every overall in town out of work. That's problem one. And its sum has sat on your napkin for six weeks, with one line missing.
lines.say: [hollow, slow, counting the empty room, a cold realisation building through the second sentence, a card laid down on problem one, the last four words a secret] Forty stools, nobody on them. Every coin that ever crossed your counter came out of an overall's pocket, and you've just put every overall in town out of work. That's problem one. And its sum has sat on your napkin for six weeks, with one line missing.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Here's the line you missed. Marco ate here. Say he took home four hundred a week. Forty of it came back over your counter, in coffee and pie. The rest went to the barber, the garage, the grocer and the bar. So when you fired him, you kept four hundred and lost forty. A great deal, for you. The barber, the garage and the grocer lost the rest, and never saw it leave.
lines.say: [quiet, the sum done out loud with a pencil, each number placed, a dry smile on for you, then slower, the last clause soft and sad] Here's the line you missed. Marco ate here. Say he took home four hundred a week. Forty of it came back over your counter, in coffee and pie. The rest went to the barber, the garage, the grocer and the bar. So when you fired him, you kept four hundred and lost forty. A great deal, for you. The barber, the garage and the grocer lost the rest, and never saw it leave.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Then every owner in town did the same sum, and every time, one of your forties walked out with their worker. Each of you kept a whole wage and lost a slice. All the slices together are the town.
lines.say: [exact, slow, the drawing repeated with a finger, the last sentence a thud] Then every owner in town did the same sum, and every time, one of your forties walked out with their worker. Each of you kept a whole wage and lost a slice. All the slices together are the town.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Money out was never out. It was going round.
lines.say: [low, slow, a lesson landing, the last word drawn out] Money out was never out. It was going round.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: You didn't fire a cook. You fired a customer who happened to know how to cook.
lines.say: [quiet, a blade of a line, the second sentence slower and plain] You didn't fire a cook. You fired a customer who happened to know how to cook.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Two economists only wrote this sum down this year, Hemenway Falk and Tsoukalas, and called it "The AI Layoff Trap": each firm keeps the whole saving and bears only a slice of the spending it destroys, and the rest lands on its rivals. One model, not yet checked by other economists. Your napkin got there first.
lines.say: [clear, a fact told as a reveal, the title given with relish, honest on the caveat, a proud grin on the last sentence] Two economists only wrote this sum down this year, Hemenway Falk and Tsoukalas, and called it "The AI Layoff Trap": each firm keeps the whole saving and bears only a slice of the spending it destroys, and the rest lands on its rivals. One model, not yet checked by other economists. Your napkin got there first.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: You'd think a boss who doubled his workers' pay had lost his mind. In 1914 Henry Ford announced a five-dollar day, doubling his workers' pay, and wrote later that his own sales depended, in a measure, on the wages he paid, because that money gets spent with storekeepers and distributors.
lines.say: [wry, setting you up, the fact plain, then a beat and the punchline dry and unhurried] You'd think a boss who doubled his workers' pay had lost his mind. In nineteen fourteen Henry Ford announced a five-dollar day, doubling his workers' pay, and wrote later that his own sales depended, in a measure, on the wages he paid, because that money gets spent with storekeepers and distributors.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Rival: So we all stop.
lines.say: [decided, a napkin held up, looking round the counter for nods] So we all stop.
lines.speaker: Rival

lines.text: Plant boss: You stop first.
lines.say: [instant, flat, a card trumped] You stop first.
lines.speaker: Plant boss

lines.text: Rival: And pay a cook while you make cars for free? No.
lines.say: [sharp, cornered, the question rising, a beat, then the no clipped] And pay a cook while you make cars for free? No.
lines.speaker: Rival

lines.text: Banker: Then nobody stops.
lines.say: [quiet, glasses off, the conclusion nobody wanted, a beat before it, crisp and clear, every word distinct, no laughter] Then nobody stops.
lines.speaker: Banker

lines.text: Everyone in town has done the sum. Everyone got it right. That's the problem.
lines.say: [cool, slow, each sentence its own beat, the last one bitter and amused] Everyone in town has done the sum. Everyone got it right. That's the problem.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: In the model, knowing is not enough, and more competition and better AI make it worse. Still unchecked.
lines.say: [grim, exact, a trap described from inside it, the last two words flat] In the model, knowing is not enough, and more competition and better AI make it worse. Still unchecked.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: The pings stop. Nobody in town can buy a car, so the boss can't pay for five hundred shifts, so the app can't pay you. You own every machine in town, and you're the one going broke. That's problem two. And at midnight you try to fix it with one more word.
lines.say: [hushed, after the silence, the chain of sos getting heavier, a dark laugh on going broke, a second card laid down, the last clause sly and low] The pings stop. Nobody in town can buy a car, so the boss can't pay for five hundred shifts, so the app can't pay you. You own every machine in town, and you're the one going broke. That's problem two. And at midnight you try to fix it with one more word.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: So you type the one job nobody in town is doing any more: CUSTOMER.
lines.say: [sly, quick, the comment section's idea, the last word deadpan] So you type the one job nobody in town is doing any more: CUSTOMER.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: The till rings, and your apron pocket goes light by the same amount, because a machine can only pay with your card. The pie just sits there.
lines.say: [deadpan, a joke performed slowly, a sigh on the pie, crisp and clear, every word distinct, no laughter] The till rings, and your apron pocket goes light by the same amount, because a machine can only pay with your card. The pie just sits there.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: A machine never calls in sick. It never eats the pie, either.
lines.say: [fond, rueful, a complete thought, the last word soft] A machine never calls in sick. It never eats the pie, either.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Plant boss: Prices will fall. They'll buy then.
lines.say: [hopeful, a little desperate, coat on in the doorway] Prices will fall. They'll buy then.
lines.speaker: Plant boss

lines.text: Rival: Buy with what?
lines.say: [flat, instant, phone in her hand, no beat at all] Buy with what?
lines.speaker: Rival

lines.text: He cuts his cars in half anyway, and nothing moves, because a price is never zero and a wage now is. So you give the money back.
lines.say: [quick on the montage, dead flat on nothing moves, cold and precise on the wage, then a shrug and a little hope on the last sentence, crisp and clear, every word distinct, no laughter] He cuts his cars in half anyway, and nothing moves, because a price is never zero and a wage now is. So you give the money back.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: You'd think a yearly cheque for residents, just for living there, is a fairy tale. Alaska has paid its eligible residents one out of oil money every year since 1982, about twelve hundred dollars this year. So you write the town one every month, out of the rent.
lines.say: [wry on the fairy tale, then fair and plain, a fact offered honestly, then generous and brisk, a pen moving fast] You'd think a yearly cheque for residents, just for living there, is a fairy tale. Alaska has paid its eligible residents one out of oil money every year since nineteen eighty-two, about twelve hundred dollars this year. So you write the town one every month, out of the rent.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Mayor: Out of whose rent?
lines.say: [sharp, sash straightened, first in the line] Out of whose rent?
lines.speaker: Mayor

lines.text: Rival: Mine.
lines.say: [sour, from behind her, a beat late, through her teeth] Mine.
lines.speaker: Rival

lines.text: It works for a week. Then the cheque runs into tills with robots behind them, and the owners spend it on more machines. It pays the bills. It doesn't change the sum.
lines.say: [bright and relieved, a shadow on the last word of the first sentence, then tracing a loop with a finger, a weary laugh on more machines, even and kind, then firm on the last sentence] It works for a week. Then the cheque runs into tills with robots behind them, and the owners spend it on more machines. It pays the bills. It doesn't change the sum.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Only the plumber and the hairdresser keep any of it, because nobody can type their jobs in. Everyone else sees that, stops waiting for the next cheque, and comes for the machines.
lines.say: [amused on the exceptions, a fond wave, then low, a drumbeat, the last word heavy] Only the plumber and the hairdresser keep any of it, because nobody can type their jobs in. Everyone else sees that, stops waiting for the next cheque, and comes for the machines.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Nobody can bring themselves to hit a smiling face. You'd think nobody had ever tried this. Between 1811 and 1816 English textile workers called Luddites smashed machines in raids on mills. They never had to look one in the face.
lines.say: [hushed, a held breath let out, half a laugh of relief, then storyteller, plain on the fact, the last sentence slow and pointed] Nobody can bring themselves to hit a smiling face. You'd think nobody had ever tried this. Between eighteen eleven and eighteen sixteen English textile workers called Luddites smashed machines in raids on mills. They never had to look one in the face.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Plant boss: Smash our machines, and the plant two towns over makes the cars. The board meets Friday noon.
lines.say: [grave, tired, a folder under his arm, the deadline flat, crisp and clear, every word distinct, no laughter] Smash our machines, and the plant two towns over makes the cars. The board meets Friday noon.
lines.speaker: Plant boss

lines.text: Marco: And if we don't smash them?
lines.say: [the wrench still in his hand, turning, the question asked for real, crisp and clear, every word distinct, no laughter] And if we don't smash them?
lines.speaker: Marco

lines.text: Plant boss: Then it makes them here. For nobody.
lines.say: [grave, tired, a beat before the last two words, flat, crisp and clear, every word distinct, no laughter] Then it makes them here. For nobody.
lines.speaker: Plant boss

lines.text: Every owner in town was right to do it. So how can the whole town be wrong?
lines.say: [puzzled, honest, the question asked for real, slow] Every owner in town was right to do it. So how can the whole town be wrong?
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: You pick neither. The app has one dial, and only you can turn it.
lines.say: [a slow smile, a secret surfacing, the last word almost a whisper] You pick neither. The app has one dial, and only you can turn it.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Rival: Mine too? All eight?
lines.say: [panicked, shouting, running past the window] Mine too? All eight?
lines.speaker: Rival

lines.text: Too far. Make every machine too dear, and the plant leaves with them.
lines.say: [wincing, quick, the last four words flat] Too far. Make every machine too dear, and the plant leaves with them.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: A machine now costs whoever rents it, every week, its rent plus the three hundred and sixty its worker used to spend at the barber, the garage and the grocer. Fire Marco today and you still keep his four hundred and lose your forty, but the three hundred and sixty goes to the app, to you, and out again as the town's cheque. Every owner feels the whole loss at last, so a machine stays only where it's better, not just cheaper.
lines.say: [satisfied, exact, the thumbnail on the napkin, the sum walked through with a pencil, a lift on to you, then slower and clear, the last four words landed one by one] A machine now costs whoever rents it, every week, its rent plus the three hundred and sixty its worker used to spend at the barber, the garage and the grocer. Fire Marco today and you still keep his four hundred and lose your forty, but the three hundred and sixty goes to the app, to you, and out again as the town's cheque. Every owner feels the whole loss at last, so a machine stays only where it's better, not just cheaper.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Mayor: And who owns the dial?
lines.say: [sharp, arms folded, a mayor's real question] And who owns the dial?
lines.speaker: Mayor

lines.text: Only you can turn it. So you give away the number: the town writes it, the dial follows the napkin, and you keep the turning, knowing every renter in town would walk the moment you touched it.
lines.say: [thoughtful, then decided, each clause a hand passing the pencil, the last word held] Only you can turn it. So you give away the number: the town writes it, the dial follows the napkin, and you keep the turning, knowing every renter in town would walk the moment you touched it.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Rival: Cheaper to hire a cook.
lines.say: [grudging, a shrug, counting her cooks onto the truck] Cheaper to hire a cook.
lines.speaker: Rival

lines.text: Friday noon, the board votes to stay.
lines.say: [quiet, a breath held, released on the last word] Friday noon, the board votes to stay.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: The two economists' model, this year, ends on the same fix as your napkin: not a basic income, but taxing the machine itself. Still unchecked.
lines.say: [clear, a verdict read with pride, a beat before the fix, honest on the caveat, the last two words plain, crisp and clear, every word distinct, no laughter] The two economists' model, this year, ends on the same fix as your napkin: not a basic income, but taxing the machine itself. Still unchecked.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: You're still the richest person in town. You just stopped being its only customer.
lines.say: [warm, a win, the second sentence slower and sly] You're still the richest person in town. You just stopped being its only customer.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Plant boss: Still cheaper than a cook?
lines.say: [mouth full, teasing, a burger in his hand] Still cheaper than a cook?
lines.speaker: Plant boss

lines.text: Marco: Cheaper than a customer?
lines.say: [from the grill, not turning round, a quick comeback, spatula up] Cheaper than a customer?
lines.speaker: Marco

lines.text: Tomorrow, when you pay for lunch, watch where the money goes. It isn't leaving. It's on its way back round.
lines.say: [close, to you, a lesson handed over gently, the last word drawn out] Tomorrow, when you pay for lunch, watch where the money goes. It isn't leaving. It's on its way back round.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: You'd think that was the sequel's fantasy. In 2025 Visa said AI agents had already completed hundreds of real transactions, in pilot trials with its partners.
lines.say: [hushed, a little spooked, a wry lift on the fantasy, the fact quick and plain] You'd think that was the sequel's fantasy. In twenty twenty-five Visa said AI agents had already completed hundreds of real transactions, in pilot trials with its partners.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: So, would you have turned the dial? Tell us in the comments. And if you'd have done the same, hit like and subscribe.
lines.say: [bright, direct, a dare on the question, a grin on the last four words] So, would you have turned the dial? Tell us in the comments. And if you'd have done the same, hit like and subscribe.
